items.body:
Fresh off a high-octane set at MARQUEE Singapore, Sub Zero Project are showing no signs of slowing down. More than a decade into their journey, the Dutch duo of Nigel Coppen and Thomas Velderman continue to push hardstyle in new directions, pairing their unmistakable sound with increasingly ambitious live concepts and collaborations.

That momentum has carried through Our World, their latest audiovisual live concept, as well as 4444 OF A KIND, their four-man project with D-Block & S-te-Fan. Their growing presence across Tomorrowland and recent collaboration with Steve Aoki on 'Promises' have also placed them firmly within a wider electronic music conversation at a time when, as the duo put it, genre boundaries are beginning to fade.

Following their explosive performance at the Marina Bay Sands megaclub, Bandwagon caught up with Sub Zero Project to talk about 4444 OF A KIND, their approach to hardstyle, the creative freedom behind their live concepts, working with Steve Aoki, and more.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

You’ve spent more than a decade making music together. When you listen back to your earliest productions, what do you hear that is still unmistakably Sub Zero Project today?

We hear the same drive to experiment and push the boundaries of hard dance that we still have today. Of course, our sound has changed a lot over the years, but we always want to come up with something fresh. We believe that this is what has made our sound recognisable over the years.

You’ve worked together for so long that fans often experience Sub Zero Project as one creative unit. What are Nigel and Thomas individually bringing to the studio that the other person probably couldn’t replicate?

Even though we always work together on music, we definitely have different strengths in the studio. Thomas is more focused on melodies and the musical side of a track, while Nigel has a strong focus on the technical side, like kicks and other small details such as sound design and creative ideas. Those different strengths complement each other really well and are a big part of how we work together.

You’ve built Our World around four distinct visual worlds alongside new music created for this chapter of Sub Zero Project. How did you come up with the concept, and how does building a narrative-driven live show affect the way you create music in the studio?

With Our World, we wanted to show people what “Our World” actually stands for, which could be anything, just like our music. Instead of coming up with one specific theme for our show, we wanted to combine very different themes and styles into one show. The same goes for our music.

It was a really fun creative process setting up this show and creating all the music that came with it. We brought the show to so many incredible places like Antwerp, Gothenburg, Mexico City, Paris, and many more.

You’ve created several distinct live concepts over the years instead of simply touring the same DJ show. What have these concepts allowed you to express that a normal Sub Zero Project festival set cannot?

The biggest difference is that our live concepts allow us to bring our full vision to life. It’s not just about the music anymore — it’s the visuals, production, and show coming together as one experience.

It also gives us a different way to work on music. We’ve always been at our best if we have a certain direction or theme that we can dive into.

4444 OF A KIND brings you together with D-Block & S-te-Fan as a dedicated four-person team rather than simply another collaboration. Its debut single, 'Waiting 4', arrived in June, following years of history between both duos. At what point did you realise there was enough chemistry between the four of you to build an entirely new identity around it?

We actually already knew this back when we made our first collaboration, 'Darkest Hour', in 2018. The chemistry was instantly there.

Fast-forward to the end of 2025, when our management came up with the idea to build a new identity between Sub Zero Project and D-Block & S-te-Fan called 4444 OF A KIND. We already knew it was going to be a smooth and fun ride working on new music.

We spent three days at a writing camp together and made more than 10 songs, which was an amazing experience.

'Darkest Hour (The Clock)' already showed how naturally your two sounds could meet. With 4444 OF A KIND, however, you’re creating music specifically as one project. What happens differently in the studio when four producers with very established identities have to decide what a new artist should sound like?

Complete creative freedom happens. With 4444 OF A KIND, we don’t go into the studio thinking, “We have to make a new Sub Zero Project or D-Block & S-te-Fan song.”

Instead, we just have fun, come up with cool stuff, and see where the process takes us. This new project is about pushing the boundaries of hard dance and playing with different genres, without limiting ourselves to one specific sound.

This year, you had a huge presence at Tomorrowland — playing the Mainstage, hosting Sub Zero Project & Friends, performing as 4444 OF A KIND, and going back-to-back with Hardwell. From your perspective, is hardstyle having a broader global moment right now, or are the boundaries between hardstyle and mainstream electronic music simply disappearing?

We definitely feel that boundaries are fading more and more. People don’t really think in genres as much as they did back in the day, which is a good thing in our opinion, and it makes it easier for certain EDM artists to play harder songs.

For us, this is an incredibly exciting time to be a music producer.

Finally, collaboration with Steve Aoki, 'Promises', reimagines NERO’s 2011 track. What made you want to revisit that particular record, and why was Steve Aoki the right producer for you to team up with?

We absolutely love the original, so once we started chatting with him, we both agreed we could do something epic with this song. We have a good connection with Steve, and this collaboration was long overdue. We’re very happy we could finally make it happen.

items.body:
At 12, Anastasha Suchin is already learning how many stories a violin can tell. She started playing at three and a half, and has since taken the instrument from concert stages to Singapore’s National Day celebrations, where she performed her own arrangement bringing together Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil songs. She has also stepped into composition with Rosie, a miniature horror tale written for toy piano and performed by Margaret Leng Tan.

Her latest chapter brought her to the big screen. In Singapore-led animated feature The Violinist, Anastasha performs as young Fei, recording pieces by Paganini and Mendelssohn alongside original music for the film. The experience saw her approach the violin not simply as a performer, but as the musical voice of a character whose story unfolds against the Japanese Occupation.

Music has taken on an even more personal role away from the stage. With her father currently in hospital, Anastasha sometimes plays for him at his bedside — continuing a relationship with music that began when he used to ferry her to violin lessons as a child. Speaking to Bandwagon, she reflects on composing Rosie, hearing herself in The Violinist for the first time, balancing school with music, and why making someone smile remains the reason she plays.

You started learning the violin when you were very young. What do you remember about first picking it up, and what made you want to keep playing?

When I was three and a half, Mum decided to let me start on the violin, as she plays the piano and envisioned us playing many duets in the future. So it was chosen for me, but I took to it very naturally and was glad to have had a nurturing and friendly first teacher, so that made me look forward to going for classes each week.

It probably did sound like “sawing wood” at first, but I’ve improved since then.

You’re balancing school, violin practice, performances, and your other interests at just 12 years old. What does a typical week look like for you, and how do you make time for everything?

I am tuition-free, and that gives me space to relax when I get home. Co-Curricular Activity days are long ones — I am in the String Ensemble at Tanjong Katong Girls’ School — and I get home at 7 PM several days a week.

I love playing with my 16-year-old black cat and am right now in the phase of experimenting with bakes and concocting fancy drinks. Practising has never been a strong point of mine. I should be able to say that I work on my instrument for several hours a day, but in truth, I actually don’t.

Instead, I tinker on the piano and guitar and also love to sing. Oops, I hope my violin teacher (Ye Lin) isn’t reading this! Sometimes I go thrift shopping on the weekends after visiting my father in hospital.

However, when I know there is an upcoming performance, I will definitely put in the time needed to do a good job on the day. Just like studying for an exam, I guess, but much more fun.

Last year, you performed a special National Day arrangement that brought together Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil songs. How did you choose those songs, and what did you want people to feel when they heard them together?

Not only am I biracial, I also have a lot of Indian friends. Our family’s favourite food is chicken biryani! I wanted each race to be represented in my little medley.

It was an easy choice — I simply selected my three favourite songs, one in each language, to make into one. My hope was to make everyone feel included and put a big smile in their hearts.

You also composed Rosie, which has since been performed internationally. Where did the idea for the piece come from, and what did creating your own musical story teach you that performing someone else’s music could not?

Rosie was composed in 2024, when I was 10.

I’ve always been fascinated by the beaked masks the Plague Doctors wore. When the request came in for an original composition to be performed by the legendary artist Margaret Leng Tan on toy piano at the Green-Wood Catacombs — on Halloween! — it seemed like the perfect opportunity to write music based on the imagery which the mask evoked.

The more I worked on it, the more it evolved, eventually becoming a miniature horror tale in four parts, including the actual use of the mask, among other accessories!

I felt free to create the story which I wanted, with full creative licence and no performance time limits. When performing someone else’s work, every dot and dash has to be observed to give respect to the composer’s intentions. So that would be the main difference between being a composer and a performer.

How did you first become involved with The Violinist, and what did you know about young Fei when you came on board?

My manager read the press release about the upcoming movie The Violinist earlier in 2025 and, by chance, the accompanying illustration of Fei resembled me! She reached out to the director, Mr Ervin, and composer, Mr Ricky, and things fell into place from there on!

We were told that Fei was a young Peranakan girl who was prodigious on the violin, and that this story was set during the Japanese Occupation.

My grandma was actually born in the forest while great-grandma ran away from troops in 1941. My grandpa’s father disappeared during the war, and it was tough days for grandpa growing up then too. These stories resonated with me.

It is very exciting to have been blessed with the part of young Fei and have a small role in this Singapore story. I still haven’t gotten over it yet!

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 🎻 Anastasha Suchin (@anastasha.suchin.violin)

What was your role in bringing young Fei to life musically, and what was the recording process like?

Mr Ricky Ho gave me a list of pieces I had to prepare for the recording. It included the super well-known Paganini Caprice No. 24 and the opening of the Mendelssohn Violin Concerto. These are works which I grew up hearing great artists play so flawlessly. Pressure was high, but I knew I would give it my best!

There was also a lovely original duet to be performed by Fei and Kai, and that was really fun for us to do as a first-time collaboration with Mark Chia. We got along really well and also had the chance to meet up again later in Vienna, where we visited Haus der Musik together!

When you were playing as Fei, did you have to imagine how this particular character would sound on the violin, rather than simply playing as yourself?

I recorded Fei’s parts over two sessions — once with Mark at YST Recording Studio in August 2025 and later on, solo at HORUS Studios, where I did the Paganini and the Mendelssohn.

Mr Ricky told me to play as myself, since I was meant to sound like Fei practising and not a seasoned adult professional violinist performing. That was very helpful in making me play more naturally.

An interesting story is that I had literally just transitioned to a full-size violin the day before recording the duet. A benefactor who wishes to remain anonymous had generously sponsored my beautiful new instrument as I was outgrowing my current one.

An Italian luthier had made one for me, and it had been sent on its way some weeks before. However, due to a typo in the address, it went on a merry-go-round to several other countries before reaching Singapore a day before recording! It was very frightening, really, and we were imagining what state it would be in upon arrival. I was also wondering whose violin to borrow for the recording should it not be playable.

Thankfully, it was carefully checked and prepared for the recording immediately upon arrival and ready to make music. It was larger than my current three-quarter size, so I remember practising on it for hours the night before, trying to get used to the new size, weight, and feel. There was definitely a little anxiety there!

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by THE VIOLINIST (@violinistmovie)

What was it like watching the finished film for the first time and hearing your own playing come from a character on screen? Was there a moment that particularly stayed with you?

It was so surreal. I would never have imagined hearing my own playing in a film, and I felt nervous as the scenes approached, but I think it went well after all.

I particularly enjoyed the duet where Fei and Kai first play together after he has been secretly taking lessons with the teacher, and the comedic comment the teacher had made about her salary.

If you’re comfortable sharing, what does playing the violin for your father at his bedside mean to you, especially now that music has become such a personal form of connection for your family?

My father was the one shuttling me to and fro violin class since I was in preschool. He was always so happy to hear me practise at home, although most classical music made him yawn. Sometimes he’d give me song requests and show me the YouTube clips. Because I play by ear, he was always so thrilled to hear me replay his favourite songs on the spot.

Funny memory: I remember once when I was lazy and refused to practise that day. He made me hold the empty violin case over my head for some time! Don’t worry, it just happened once.

Now that he is in hospital, it’s time for me to do what I can for my father. Mum plays the recording of the Sunset Sonata performance for him to hear, and I play the violin for him at times by the bedside. Even if he cannot express it, I know he can hear it, as there are responsive signs from him each time.

When we are not there, we leave a mobile phone with different genres of music playing for him several hours a day — from classical music to The Beatles to old songs of P. Ramlee.

Finally, after experiencing music through competitions, major stages, arranging, composing, film, and something so personal, has your answer changed when someone asks you: “Why do you play the violin?”

The enduring reason why I play the violin is because I enjoy seeing the looks of delight on people’s faces as they hear me play live and knowing that I have made someone smile that day.

items.body:
BABYMONSTER have wrapped up two sold-out nights at Kyocera Dome Osaka, welcoming 90,000 fans to the latest stop of their world tour. The K-pop girl group took over the venue on 22 and 23 September, marking their first-ever performances at the dome.

As the lights went down, fans across the venue rose to their feet to welcome BABYMONSTER, whose opening performance of 'WE GO UP' kicked off the night with a full live band and the members performing with handheld microphones.

The group kept the energy going with 'SHEESH' and 'DRIP', both of which have surpassed 100 million cumulative streams in Japan, alongside tracks from their third mini-album, 춤 (CHOOM).

For the special dome shows, BABYMONSTER expanded their setlist with 'Ghost', their first original Japanese song, viral track 'REALLY LIKE YOU', and latest release 'SUGAR HONEY ICE TEA'. Individual solo stages also gave each member a chance to spotlight their vocals, rap, and performance skills.

The scale of the dome was matched by an equally massive production. Cinematic VCRs punctuated the set, while lasers, pyrotechnics, fog, and a sprawling stage transformed the venue throughout the night. Across the stands, fans added to the spectacle with waves of synchronised light sticks.

BABYMONSTER also spent plenty of time connecting directly with their Japanese fans. The members spoke in Japanese throughout the concert without interpreters and even worked Osaka dialect into their interactions with the crowd.

During the encore, the group boarded moving carts to get closer to fans around the dome. The audience's response eventually brought BABYMONSTER back out for a second encore, extending the celebration through one final round of performances.

The concerts capped off the group's Japan tour, which began in Kobe in July and comprised 11 shows across six cities. A total of 200,000 fans attended the run, while the finale at Kyocera Dome Osaka was broadcast live via WOWOW.

The dome debut also marked an emotional milestone for the group. Japanese members ASA and RUKA reflected on seeing the venue filled with fans after finally reaching a stage they had long dreamed of performing on.

"From the very first moment onstage, we felt so overwhelmed that we thought we might cry. Seeing the fans fill every seat made us realise once again just how many people love us," they shared.

"Every one of these moments is possible thanks to all our fans, who have always supported us without wavering. We hope to continue moving forward with you and create even more wonderful memories together."

The milestone follows BABYMONSTER's growing live presence in Japan, from attracting 46,000 attendees to their first fan meeting in 2024 to drawing 250,000 in 2025. With another 200,000 attendees across this year's Japan tour, their cumulative live attendance in the country is now approaching 500,000.

BABYMONSTER launched their second world tour, 2026-27 BABYMONSTER WORLD TOUR [춤 (CHOOM)], in Seoul in June. The group are set to continue the tour across Asia, Oceania, South America, North America, and Europe, with 30 shows across 18 cities planned in total. An additional Hong Kong concert has also been confirmed for 10 January.

items.body:
Lola Amour and Jan Roberts are looking back at what could have been in their first collaboration, 'Tapos Na Ba (Tayong Dalawa)'.

Released on 25 September, the folk-pop track sees the two Filipino acts reexamine a relationship that has already ended, turning memories into imagined scenarios and unanswered questions about how things might have turned out differently.

Rather than simply yearning for a former love, 'Tapos Na Ba (Tayong Dalawa)' finds its narrator confronting the lingering "what ifs" that follow a breakup — including the possibility of a life where the relationship never ended.

The song was written by Roberts and Lola Amour frontman Pio Dumayas, with the composition credited to Roberts alongside Lola Amour members Jeffrey Abueg, Emilio Dumayas, Pio, Zoe Gonzales, Angelo Mesina, Raffy Perez, and David Yuhico.

Produced by Lola Amour, the track was recorded by Macoy Manuel, mixed by CUURLEY, and mastered by Jett Galindo. It also features Roi Mendones on trumpet.

'Tapos Na Ba (Tayong Dalawa)' arrives as Lola Amour continue to bring their blend of pop, funk, and indie music to audiences beyond the Philippines. The seven-piece are set to return to Singapore for the Singapore Formula 1 Grand Prix, joining a lineup that includes Janet Jackson, Goo Goo Dolls, Zara Larsson, CORTIS, and more.

Roberts, meanwhile, released his debut five-track EP, Pusong Pabrika, in August. The project was preceded by 'Selepono' with jikamarie and 'Kung Masusunod' with Johnoy Danao, the latter of which is nominated for Folk Song of the Year at the 2026 Filipino Music Awards.

items.body:
Gehlee Dangca is coming home. After three years of living and pursuing her dreams in South Korea, the Filipina singer and former UNIS member will return to the Philippines on 29 September as she begins a new chapter in her career as a solo artist.

Gehlee is set to pursue opportunities both in the Philippines and internationally, while also returning home to finish school. Fans can expect to see more of the young artist across Philippine media and entertainment through upcoming appearances, projects, and activities.

Gehlee first caught international attention through Universe Ticket, the global survival programme that formed K-pop girl group UNIS. Her journey began after SBS approached Universal Records Philippines to scout Filipino talents for the competition.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by gehlee 🌸 (@gehlee_dangca)

After securing a spot on the programme, Gehlee emerged as one of its standout contestants, garnering the highest number of votes and ultimately taking the fourth debut spot among the eight members selected for UNIS.

She officially debuted with the group in March 2024 and spent the next two and a half years based in South Korea, building her experience as a performer and K-pop artist while reaching audiences around the world.

With her return to the Philippines, Gehlee will continue working with Universal Records Philippines as her recording label. GLXY Talent Management, the talent management arm of Universal Records, and Star Horizon TV Production will oversee her management in the Philippines.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by GLXY Talent Management (@glxymanagement)

Both management teams have supported Gehlee's career since before her time in South Korea and will continue working together to develop opportunities for the singer locally.

Gehlee also joins Universal Records and GLXY's growing roster of international talents, which includes Korean stars Kim Myung Soo (L) and Choi Bo Min, as well as Thai internet personality Aon Somrutai.

With international performing experience under her belt, Gehlee's homecoming will give her a chance to reconnect with Filipino fans while continuing to build her career beyond the Philippines. More details on Gehlee's upcoming projects, media appearances, and activities are expected to be announced soon.

items.body:
Elton John is set to christen Apple Music Hall, a new live music venue in London, with a surprise opening performance.

The British music icon will take the stage at the 600-capacity venue at Battersea Power Station on 28 September, marking his first public UK performance in more than three years.

John's performance kicks off a packed opening season that will also feature Baby Keem, Skye Newman, Troye Sivan, Arlo Parks, Burna Boy, Chase & Status, and Charli xcx through December.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Apple Music (@applemusic)

Tickets are available via Apple Music Hall's official website.

The show follows John's appearance at Rock in Rio in Brazil on 7 September. His last public UK performance was at Glastonbury Festival in June 2023, where he wrapped up his Farewell Yellow Brick Road tour.

The singer is no stranger to Battersea Power Station. He previously played a private concert at the London landmark in 2014 to mark the building's residential and commercial redevelopment.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Apple Music (@applemusic)

Apple Music Hall is equipped with a 48-speaker spatial audio system and a customisable 38-foot-wide stage. The space also houses two dedicated recording and mix studios and is wired for 16 or more cameras alongside a purpose-built broadcast control room, allowing performances to be captured for audiences beyond the venue.

Apple opened its London headquarters at Battersea Power Station in 2022, with the site also housing studios used by Apple Music Radio's London-based hosts.

For the new venue, Apple has partnered with UK promoter Communion ONE to support bookings and promotion.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Apple Music Hall (@applemusichall)

"Apple Music Hall is a fantastic venue, like nothing fans will have ever seen before," Communion ONE Managing Director Mazin Tappuni said. "The production quality is world class, livestreaming to fans across the world, from a live room where every square foot has the artist and their fans in mind."

Check out Apple Music Hall's opening season lineup below:

28 September — Elton John

2 October — Baby Keem

7 October — Skye Newman

13 October — Troye Sivan

22 October — Arlo Parks

29 October — Burna Boy

26 November — Chase & Status

2 December — Charli xcx

Swim by BTS wins Best K-Pop at the 2026 #VMAs. pic.twitter.com/sGlrQXczcW

— About Music (@AboutMusicYT) September 28, 2026

The septet's 'Swim' beat out tracks from Ella Langley, HUNTR/X: EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and REI AMI, Madonna and Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Dean, PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson, and RAYE for Song of the Year.

In the Best K-Pop category, BTS were nominated alongside BLACKPINK's 'JUMP', CORTIS' 'REDRED', KATSEYE's 'PINKY UP', LE SSERAFIM featuring j-hope of BTS with 'SPAGHETTI', and LISA's 'Dream' featuring Kentaro Sakaguchi.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CBS (@cbstv)

LISA, meanwhile, scored a win of her own with 'Dream', taking home Best Pop against nominees including Ariana Grande, Charli xcx, Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter, Tate McRae, and Taylor Swift. LISA also performed during the ceremony.

Elsewhere, Madonna emerged as the night's biggest winner, collecting seven awards in total. The pop icon was named Artist of the Year and also took home Best Dance, Best Collaboration with Sabrina Carpenter for 'Bring Your Love', Best Cinematography, Best Choreography, Best Long Form Video, and Best Album for Confessions II.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CBS (@cbstv)

Swift took home Video of the Year for 'The Fate of Ophelia' and Best Direction for 'Opalite'. She was also presented with the inaugural Artist Director Honors, after which she premiered the self-directed music video for her new track 'Patient Zero'.

Other winners included Sienna Spiro, who was voted Best New Artist; Cardi B and Kehlani, who won Best Hip-Hop for 'Safe'; Bruno Mars, who picked up Best R&B for 'I Just Might'; Olivia Rodrigo, who won Best Alternative for 'the cure'; Bad Bunny, who took Best Latin for 'NUEVAYoL'; and Ella Langley, who won Best Country for 'Choosin’ Texas'.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Video Music Awards (@vmas)

Ariana Grande's 'Hate That I Made You Love Me' was named Song of Summer and also won Best Visual Effects, while PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson's 'Stateside' picked up Best Art Direction. Sabrina Carpenter's 'House Tour' won Best Editing.

Beyond the awards, the night featured performances from Madonna, LISA, RAYE, Sienna Spiro, Shaboozey, Gunna, GENER8ION, and Yung Lean. Kacey Musgraves paid tribute to Dolly Parton, while RAYE, sombr, and Teddy Swims honoured George Michael.

items.body: By the third instalment of their Is Noise series, TAKAAT [pronounced tuh-cot and meaning “noise” in the Tuareg language Tamashek] have moved further from the raw collision of Tuareg guitar and punk that initially defined the project. The trio has become a duo here, without Souleymane Ibrahim’s live drums or any vocals. Vol. 3 is more exploratory and searching, less concerned with songs than with seeing how far Ahmoudou Madassane and Mikey Coltun can stretch their shared musical language. Drum machines, drones and field recordings move into the space left behind. The four-part Ijit N’elwan begins almost by withholding TAKAAT altogether. “Ijit N’elwan 1” opens with field recordings and remains a brief, ambient introduction, establishing a sense of place before amplification takes over. The second part strips things down to an extended, heavily distorted guitar passage whose sustained tones eventually push the track into drone territory. “Ijit N’elwan 3” initially reveals something bluesier in Madassane’s playing, but gradually acquires greater weight and distortion as it progresses, while the final part heads somewhere more psychedelic. Coltun’s comments in the accompanying interview help explain why this expansion feels natural. He draws a connection between the trance-like repetition at the heart of Tuareg guitar music and drone, as well as between the distortion of contemporary Takamba—music blasted through overloaded radios and megaphone speakers—and the punk, noise and experimental music that shaped his own listening. On Vol. 3, those affinities no longer need to be announced: they have become part of the music’s vocabulary. There is also a deliberate sense of risk. Each new TAKAAT EP enters a different world while remaining recognisably part of the same universe, and Vol. 3 takes that idea further than its predecessors. The duo format makes the music feel simultaneously more exposed and more open-ended as well as restless and unafraid of charting new territory. To make sense of the noise we reached out directly to TAKAAT with Mikey Coltun answering our questions. Across the three Is Noise volumes, TAKAAT has moved quite quickly from the raw Tuareg guitar and punk energy of Vol. 1, through the live-to-tape Tinariwen reworkings of Vol. 2, to the drones, drum machines, field recordings and much denser noise of Vol. 3. Was this evolution something you imagined when TAKAAT began, or has each volume simply opened up possibilities for the next one? Mikey Coltun: It’s been a mix of both. We knew there was a lot to explore sonically when Ahmoudou and I started the band but to what extent was a bit more unknown until we started touring and experimenting both live and during the recording process. Each Is Noise is recorded to tape. That’s kinda the overall concept. Similarly if you look at the album art (shout out to our designer Can Misirlioglu) throughout the volumes the structure remains the same but is a different perspective and zoomed out throughout each volume. This was intentional from the beginning as it relates to the music and the progression of each Is Noise volume. Mikey, you’ve drawn a connection between the distortion of modern Takamba—particularly the tehardent amplified through blown-out radios—and the noise and experimental music you grew up with in Washington, D.C. [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. On Vol. 3, do those traditions actually meet in the way you make sound, or are they still distinct references that you bring into TAKAAT from different directions? Mikey Coltun: There’s definitely all of those influences – Takamba, punk, noise and experimental music present on Vol. 3. Similar to later era John Coltrane, a lot of Tuareg music is drone music at its core. With Tuareg guitar music, a simple chord structure with trance-like rhythms and melodies often played for long periods of time is no different than the spirituality of drone music and this is something Ahmoudou and I were interested in exploring. Taking our guitar and bass and blasting it through amps creating different sonic distortions can be also heard when seeing Takamba music live but instead of the guitar amps you have a blown out radio receiver roaring through megaphone speakers. As Ahmoudou has put it, TAKAAT is the “feeling of being in the desert at night.” Vol. 3 also changes the basic instrumental architecture of TAKAAT: drum machines, drone synths and manipulated field recordings become central alongside Ahmoudou’s guitar and Mikey’s bass. What interested you about moving away from the more recognisable guitar/bass/drums setup of the earlier volumes, and how did that change the way you approached improvisation? Mikey Coltun: It’s important for Ahmoudou and I to be experimenting musically and taking risks. We talk a lot about how Taureg legends Tinariwen pushed, what Tuareg music is, and what we’re doing with TAKAAT is breaking the expectations of the known Tuareg rock sound. We want each record to push into a different world while still staying in the universe of TAKAAT. This goes the same with our shows. Each tour Ahmoudou and I want to present something different with TAKAAT. The first few tours we did the trio, last tour was a duo presenting a loud drone and blown out drum machines, and next tour will be something different too. We’re taking risks and we want people to come take these risks with us. This is the only way to push out of comfort zones and create something new. You’ve described the trust developed through eight years of playing together as something that allows TAKAAT to take risks, while Mikey has also spoken about the project as a return to a more DIY world where there is less pressure to perform in a particular way [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. Does TAKAAT give you a kind of freedom that you don’t necessarily have in Mdou Moctar—and has that freedom changed the way you listen and respond to one another when you play? Mikey Coltun: It was really clear early on touring together with Mdou Moctar that Ahmoudou and I were excited by similar music. I brought a lot of different types of bands on tour with Mdou. All of the music is by groups and artists that I love. While some of the groups could have been challenging to listeners it was important to me to draw that connection with what we were doing with Mdou. Mdou’s music was different and challenging to some in the Tuareg wedding scene in Agadez, Niger. With a lot of these bands I brought on tour I found Ahmoudou’s interest peaked. Whenever there was an opportunity on tour I would take him to see sound installations, free jazz groups, modern art, etc… and he really does appreciate that. Because Ahmoudou and I have similar interests sonically, there is a lot of trust and comfortability to experiment and try new things together with TAKAAT. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Cuatro Piraguas started “La Cumbia del Jardinero” after a sleepless night and a small gardening episode at Villa Plagwitz in Leipzig, which suits a debut album called En vela, Spanish for a night spent awake. The quartet take their name from the dugout canoes of Latin America and the Caribbean, and work across Afro-Peruvian rhythm, Colombian Caribbean folklore and the music of Venezuela and Brazil. Celia Regina sings and plays cuatro, with Mauricio Vivas on accordion, guitar and cuatro, Thomas Campbell Tyler on bass and Felix Zehdnicker on percussion. A year of live shows shaped the song, and the recording with their friend Max Gruener adds clarinet and trombone from Eldar Tsalikov and Marleen Dahms, plus backing vocals from friends. The band name two Colombian influences: Totó la Momposina, the singer from the river island of Mompox who died in May aged 85, and Cali-born songwriter Marta Gómez. The verses fill a gardener’s morning with small chores done with affection: coffee at the window, water against a dry spell, an ear for what each plant has to say. The chorus switches to labour, alternating between a gardener who works all day and a wheelbarrow that keeps rolling. The band read that routine as a picture of their own debut: gardens and records both take time and care before anything flowers. En vela is due this autumn, and vinyl, CD and download pre-orders run through their crowdfunding page until 27 September. Two nights before it closes, they play a free gig at Kulturbar froelich & herrlich, beneath Leipzig’s Westflügel puppet theatre on Friday 25 September. Stream “La Cumbia del Jardinero” HERE and support the release of En Vela through the band’s crowdfunding page at THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Cuatro Piraguas – Cumbia del Jardinero appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Drone music is nothing new of course having existed in ancient musical forms ranging from ancientHindustani and Carnatic styles to Japanese gagaku, Byzantine chants and Scottish bagpipes however interms of more modern Western music it really got a foothold in the early world of electronic musicwhen La Monte Young began a new minimalist experimentalism that has continued to the current day. Bythe late 60s acts like Finland's The Sperm and Germany's Kluster soon to be Cluster as well aslesser known artists like Italy's Harry Bertoia were really warming up to the possibilities of darkambient sounds set to a sustained note. A handful of acts began to follow suit however oneinteresting artifact from the early 70s was the album PLANES by the duo of GREGOR C�RTEN & ANSEMROGMANS who only entered the musical arena to record this sole album before C�RTEN would move on tothe world of visual art and painting while ROGMANS would become a school teacher and choir director.For having no prior history and no future releases, PLANES is a surprisingly cool album that fitright into the burgeoning progressive electronic and Krautrock sweeping the German music scene ofthe era. This album came out in 1974 and featured two sprawling tracks that each swallowed up anentire side of the vinyl release. Following in the footsteps of Kluster, Eliane Radigue and La MonteYoung, GREGOR C�RTEN & ANSEM ROGMANS crafted a haunting display of electronically hypnotic dronefreakiness that seemed to be part Kluster, part early Klaus Schulze and part A.R. & Machines. Whiledrone music is hit and miss with most acts missing the mark of what it takes to deliver attentionkeeping minimalism that can sustain an album's worth of material, PLANES is an interesting rarityfrom the era that offers a nice escapist's paradise into a sonic playground that finds just enoughspices to keep it all enthralling.The first side simply titled "Planes I" sounds like a musical shaving session with a buzzing soundthat sounds like an electric razor that establishes itself a good while before haunting wordlessvocalizations and creepy organs find themselves embellished by a series of random electronic effectsand tape manipulations. While the droning effects are in the forefront, the tenebrous organ riffsand lugubrious vocals are quite chilling as the track slowly drifts through its 18-minute plusduration. The contemplative buzzing mediation adds that certain uneasiness while the pacifyingpredictability simultaneously soothes the soul. The second track titled "Planes II" offers a totallydifferent spin albeit in a similarly themed droning drift that also lasts just slightly longer thanthe 18-minute mark. This one opens with a tinny repetitious guitar twang that slowly changes pitchup and down the scale and then joined in by a slow monotonous organ drone that also incrementallyflows glacially. This particular effect is very much out of the Achim Reichel playbook but yetsounds totally unique in this context. Drone music can be quite dull if not done properly but these guys really knew how to generate analbum's worth of exhilarating drone music by creating a fascinating slow building tension that couldhave been one of the inspirations of the later post-rock. The album artfully incorporates the tonesand flavors of progressive electronic, especially the Berlin School variety along with Krautrocktechniques only funneled into a more minimalist drone style of slowly unfolding musical innovations.The production is very good and the album is best experienced loud and on a good speaker where youcan feel the reversing micro-changes of the pitches which offer an entire body experience. It's aninteresting underground relic of Germany's fertile musical underground and one that shouldn't bemissed by lover's of electronic escapist music. While Kluster is the most brandished reference, thismusic isn't nearly as bleak and industrial sounding and more detached in a creepy drugged outexperience way.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — In the early 1980s, German musician Peter Frohmader, creator of the famous Nekropolis trilogy, teamed up with none other than Artemiy Artemiev. Like Frohmader, Artemiev was an electronic musician, but he was also the son of Eduard Artemiev, a pioneer of Russian electronic music who had composed, among other works, the soundtrack for Andrei Tarkovsky's film Solaris.Here, each playing a synthesizer, they weave a subtle sonic tapestry; utilizing electric guitar, bass, and gong percussion, Frohmader shapes a progressive symphony that evokes the "space rock" era of Pink Floyd, the psychedelia of the band Gong, and the harmonic style of Klaus Schulze. What makes the work novel and original is the way guitar variations play against synthesizer loops, much like an overcast sky filled with countless clouds, where rays of light occasionally break through the monochromatic sheen, tearing the canvas here and there to complete the panorama. Hints of rock and blues emerge, improvisations set against the unwavering electronic foundations, creating a truly unique texture.Later on, it takes on a percussive intensity as the guitar launches into psychedelic jams, almost as if Steve Hillage had stepped onto the scene, and the term "electronic progressive rock" acquires a new meaning; the fusion becomes even more deeply intertwined in "Space Icon." "Mir" is the second track; in Russian, it means "Peace," but it can also signify "Universe" or "World." This double meaning, this duality, suits the track's music perfectly; in contrast to the expansive opening, the sound is relaxed, mysterious, and introspective. Electronic music evokes sensations and moods that are not always associated with words, at least not initially, yet it is that secondary level of meaning that we are attempting to explore here.Once again, layered synthesizers and gongs serve an ethereal melody that seems to evoke the presence of a hidden soprano, while "Channeling", the third track, is more tribal, primitive, organic, and minimalist; it calls to mind the East and reminded me of Brand X's percussion, as Frohmader actually plays fretless bass on this track. Turning to the East, "Zen Garden" fully immerses us in that realm; one can picture Pierre Moerlen and his percussion work with Gong, yet set within a context where everything seems to float. The synthesizers resemble currents of wind, and simultaneously pan flutes, reinforcing a sense of earthly connection. "Space Icon" orbits between these two poles: the earthly realm and the space beyond Earth."Cosmic Jungle" is an expansive closing track that fuses the jungle and the cosmos; it gradually becomes saturated with dissonance as the sounds of birds morph into tribal drums, contrasting sharply with those distinctly electric dissonances, before circling back to the minimalism of the opening, ultimately concluding with an ambient finish reminiscent of Delia Derbyshire and the Standard Music Library.Recorded between Art Recording Studio in Moscow and Studio Nekropolis in Munich, this collaborative album culminates in a projection of Russo-German influences that stands as an icon of that very fusion.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Right off the bat, playing the harmonium like a classical piano hints at the atypical nature of this album. Five Suns is like an explosion containing multiple explosions within itself, much like fireworks that conceal other pyrotechnics, releasing them at just the right moment. Guitar and organ flesh out the trio's sound, which surges forward with the Mellotron in Part 2 of the Five Suns suite.We are talking about the English band Guapo; they constantly shift and mutate, yet their musical vision remains consistently compelling and challenging, both for the musicians themselves and for the listener. Perhaps therein lies the secret: while their previous album, Great Sage, Equal of Heaven, was a duo featuring a guest saxophonist, here, as a stripped-down trio, they sound richer and darker. They evoke a King Crimson-esque vibe infused with dissonant jazz-rock, while also bringing to mind the dense fusion of the Norwegian band Red Kite and the psychedelic space rock of Monomith.The fact that both Matt Thompson and Daniel O'Sullivan alternated between guitar and samplers, while Dave Smith varied the drum rhythms, contributed to the suite's unpredictability. This was followed by subtle moments of counterpoint between the bass and the Rhodes, which in turn served as a foundation for new drum solos; the drums never stood alone for long, however, before the guitar rejoined the mix. Just when the balance seemed to tip toward Mahavishnu-style fusion, that compulsion for avant-garde composition returned, defining the entirety of Part 3 of Five Suns, as dissonance and psychedelia took center stage.Another key point for me was their ability to know exactly when to break up repetitive sections with rhythm changes; every element had its own purpose and appeared at precisely the right moment. There is room for groove in Five Suns, just as at other moments chaos takes over and things spiral out of control, a chaos that ultimately proves to be controlled, much like improvisation in classic jazz, a passage that highlights precisely the strength of the other."Five Suns," Part 4, with its more prominent organ and contrapuntal drumming, sounds more progressive and thrilling, building to a near-dramatic climax reminiscent of Yndi Halda's Enjoy Eternal Bliss. The fifth and final part carries an aura of danger and suspense; as the distorted guitar gives way to the keyboards, the music plunges into the void of an organ solo lost in an unfathomable abyss."Mictlan" possesses the freshness, lightness, and fluidity of a unique piece, as if casting off the heavy burden of belonging to such a dense suite; the Rhodes floats freely, and the drums follow suit in an exercise that is as playful as it is anarchic. Here, the Mellotron reigns supreme alongside the distorted bass, representing the "rock 'n' roll" side of Guapo's avant-garde jazz-rock, while the music vibrates and sways, accelerating to perfectly complement what stands as the flip side of Five Suns. It wouldn't be complete without the other side of the coin, "Topan", where they deconstruct fusion in the style of Eskaton, with their degraded harmonies, only to end with the same mystery with which we began: an open-ended conclusion that serves as the best guarantee of an imminent return.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Germany's pre-eminent Jazz-Fusion guitar player is back with an album that shows his openness and adaptability to all of the recent technologic trends in music. 1. "Hypnotic Pignose" (4:27) my how rapidly-advancing technologies have affected the sounds of musical instruments. Nearly none of the instruments used here sound anything like those we heard in Volker's earlier albums--even just three years before! The bass, the way the drums and percussion sound, the keys, of course, and the guitars--all of it are so much different, all of it allowing an all-pervasive underlying "funk" sound to dominate. The music is funky as much due to sound as to changes in playing styles (though those too have been affected). (9.125/10)2. "Circus Gambet" (4:41) a clean, electric sound that finds Volker's music approaching the sound of both Yacht Rock and Smooth Jazz. The musicianship is still jazz-strong, still highly-skilled and nuanced, but the overall feel and sound is so much more "easy" on the ears and brain. And, again: there is funk here without even seeming to try! The synthesizer solo in the third minute definitely gives away the effect of American Black Funk Soul/R&B bands like Earth, Wind & Fire, Kool & The Gang, and Smooth Jazz proponent Bob James. At the same time Volker's guitar virtuosity is not something to be overlooked: he has definitely taken the technologies to heart while figuring out how to use them to his advantage in his guitar expression. (9.125/10)3. "Hallo Albert" (3:36) a gentle, comforting sound palette in which Volker and trombonist Albert Mangelsdorff trade gentle, sensitive solos (Volker's in both electric and acoustic). Almost Prog Folk feeling. (9/10)4. "Remember Gereba" (3:08) a nice African percussion jam opens this one for the first 1:10 before fading away to be replaced by an acoustic-guitar-accompanied trombone-led version of a children's lullaby (or famous limerick). The percussion jam is re-faded in for the last minute to finish the song. Weird. (8.875/10)5. "Sister Matic" (3:49) sassy funk-lite with a Sesame-Street feeling element over which Volker tries to shred with all of the latest effects of psychedelic guitarists (e.g. those used by Ernie Isley, Todd Rundgren, Frank Zappp, and Neal Schon) It works, kind of--though it does feel a little trite and contrived. (8.875/10)6. "Oriente" (6:06) serious piano and electric piano working with bass, guitar, and Jay Nay's reflective drums. An interesting and not-altogether definable or consistent construct, there are several odd motifs knitted together within and over which Volker lashes out with a variety of guitar sounds, styles, and volumes. Keyboard maestro Rainer Br�ninghaus shows his skills and range here while the rhythm corps do an admirable job of following the script of the odd composition. Easily the best, most refreshing Jazz-Rock Fusion tune on the album--though it is also the oddest/most out-of-place. There are echoes of FOCUS/JAN AKKERMAN in this one. (9.25/10)7. "Bahia Next Yera" (5:36) the percussion/rhythm track that this song opens with sounds like something from a PAT METHENY album--something with a bit of a World Music influence and flavor to it. Rich electric piano and dual-guitar-and-keyboard harmonized melody lines flow over the top in the coolest, tightest three-and-four-part weave. It's kind of smooth jazz and yet some of the most sophisticated, classically-informed world-music/blues-rock fusion you'll likely hear. Again, Pat Metheny group renderings keep popping into my head the further we go into this as well as Weather Report and John Abercrombie, Larry Carlton, and Ralph Towner stuff as well. (9.25/10)8. "Tribut" (1:02) banjo, calliope, and both Moog and wah-wahed bass lines woven with shakers and broom to make a jazzy C&W tune. Clever and cute! (4.5/5)9. "Let's Say Windmill" (4:35) Shaft-like percussion weave with bass and electric piano chord play sets the stage for Volker's concise electric and keyboard--until 1:20 when a very sudden wonky bass sound jumps in and turns the mutha out: into a very funky tune over which Volker becomes the rhythm guitarist and Rainer becomes the lead instrumentalist while Jay Nay carries a Disco-lite drum beat to go with the funky bass of Hans Peter Stroer and Rainer's keyboard. Motif changes continue to move between fine country-folk fare and stinky funk until the former finishes things off. Interesting! And quite enjoyable! A fourth one in a row that will need multiple listens to make sense of. (9.125/10)10. "Saturnalia" (2:41) multiple guitar tracks, some acoustic, some electric, one, in the center, doing its best early Pat Metheny ("It's for You"--which won't come out for another five years) impression. (Does this indicate that Pat must have heard some Volker Kriegel in his European travels and collaborations? I think it only makes sense.) By the end both electric and acoustic guitars have taken their turns in the lead position. Beautiful Ralph Towner/ New Chatauqua-like fare. (4.625/5)Total Time: 39:41All tracks by Kriegel except 4 by Gereba, Kriegel, 6 by Gilberto Gil, arranged by Kriegel, Hans Stroer, 8 by Kriegel, Hans Stroer and 10 by Hans StroerA-/five stars; a definite minor masterpiece of up-to-date Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion. Volker Kriegel is definitely one artist who keeps up and keeps pushing the envelope with his virtuosic guitar skills and song-construction abilities.

items.body: Review by Stroumpf — Imbued with post metal and symphonic movements cores of death, black and abstract math metal fuse in a Large Orgone Collider -a showcase of overpowering inventiveness and technical bravuraStephen Jarrett's despondent, hyper-agile, 'psychological' guitar narrates and nervously navigates the manic, fluctuating surreal world of external horrors it builds: a landscape of dread and overwhelming doom textures to simulate a complete eclipse. As sonic, technically overpowering dramaturge, master-narrator and litterateur withing the distinct sub-genre of abstract tech metal, he shares an astonishing conceptual and technical lineage with Robert Fripp and Steve Hackett.With a melancholy anthropomorphic elephant holding a mandolin on the album cover (and who does not know that African forest elephants disperse the seeds of the ebony trees from which premium guitar fingerboards are made), one is likely to think of a surreal Jazz festival poster. 'Jazzy' and surreal in an abstract tech death metal way, linear through-composed the ride is going to be, starting with an instrumental accelerando that could be an after-thought to The Goliath's 'Vomited Hyacinths'. The album asserts its individuality with the titular second track 'Joyless Parson' which forms together with the razor-sharp Slayer-esque head cleaner 'Mourn' (an instant classic of furious beastliness) and the monolithic 'The Void of course' (Voc) -a non-formulaic center piece and multi-movement epic- the three pillars of this piece of avant-guard art.With the analytical prose-anti-poetry telling us about the wretched and tortured joyless parson, who is kept alive by a contemptuous life force, his pastoral illusions ('fantastic lies worth repeating' up until his 'feeling unworthy of pleasure [?] guarding alone a cache of treasure which no one values and no one visits'), there seems not much space for emotional growth: nevertheless, the musical representation of a hypnotic decent into human depravity and existential paralysis offers us a breath-taking juxtaposition of intense mathematical dissonance and serene, sorrowful classical melodicism and haunting chamber melancholy (piano and cello) prefiguring their 2024 masterwork 'Pleroma'. Abandon expectations of genre-typical, traditional metal anthems with refrains along a uniform hyper-fast blast beats-driven grid (though Orgone can do anthemic, world-shattering riffs and head-banging stuff, too). The guitar work (and the guitar does all the work) centers on non-repeating distinct upper register micro-phrases -shall we call them micro-riffs or 'micro-memes?'-, each bar organically and erratically mutating into the next. The ever-shape-shifting guitar work will mimic and impressively dramatize how a hapless individual racks his brain. Layers of Black Sabbath DNA lie bare: knotty, sludgy riffage, almost minimalistic, primitive playing style and muddy mid-range crunch make appearances. But it's Tony Iommi on amphetamines: everything is shot through, imbued and augmented with expressive, breathtakingly inertia-free fretboard swash-buckling, rapid-fire interval leaps, chaotic chromatic shifts, attacking pushing micro-timing driving the beast, counter-melodic playing and harsh dissonances. Jarrett's anti-traditional soloing is existential protagonist, agitator, catalyst and jumpingly associative propellant. Beside itself in a mental flow, it is its own antagonist, commenting, probing, cajoling, shooting distracting flares; it falters and picks itself up again, flays the strings, wields justice on the hoof, runs evasive maneuvers, inserts evocative moments of respite and serenity expanding with soaring climaxes of staggering beauty (again and non-repetitively again). The guitar work literally whips and drags the band along, until heights of despair turn into blazing technical and melodical fireworks.'Void of course', an astrological term apparently refers to the moon's transitioning between Zodiac signs and its running into emptiness symbolizes a time of [self-imposed] isolation. The 14 min long song serves as the album's emotional and sonic anchor. Much of JP's runtime is therefore spent in sinuous, drifting fluctuations, patient, lumbering builds, a suffocating crawl forming heavy, expansive doom and echoey post metal atmospheres before straight-ahead aggression strikes again up to successions of disorienting peripeties, drawn-out climaxes and releases, culminating in some grotesque dance of the near-dead and a very painfully evocative, psychotic Caspar Br�tzmann-like pingy, plinky-ploink disintegration fest. A heart-breaking atmospheric drop into a mental chasm follows with a shuddersome coda. Most guitarists would have exhausted and repeated their vocabulary of tricks and phrases several songs ago. Multi-instrumentalist and ego-free gentleman shredder Jarrett, however, up to the messy, slightly fuzzy, synoptic round-up track 'Circulated Treason' that even contains slivers of uplifting, playful music, he just keeps on giving. As the architect of its own nightmare, he layers chaotic, multi-tracked arpeggios that are like structural fractures. Drummer Justin Wharton utilizes staccato shifts, sudden stops and accelerations to sound out the psychological load with servings of disorienting time-signatures and something akin to American Primitivism while (even) the deft vocal delivery adds vocal percussion, atmosphere and inimitable lyrical heft.'Joyless Parson' is bleaker, more doom-laden and was recorded only 1 year after its equally inspired, very, very fast predecessor 'The Goliath'. The slowing down allows breathing space for the instruments and incredible skills to shine. Together they stand closer to the brain-frying, punishing mathcore debut 'Accumulator' than to the multi-voiced, genre-fluid, maximalist super production 'Pleroma' [2024] though the idioms, and symphonic sweep are already manifest.Oh well, the album lacks a bit of sound engineering clarity (especially compared to the follow-up 'Pleroma') -but so what? Hey, we know what it is meant to sound like and that's all that matters! An utterly uncompromising 96%

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Fuchs is, above all, Hans-J�rgen and Ines, partners both on stage and off. The couple had already collaborated under the name "Ines" in the 2000s, releasing four captivating albums in which the young Ines Fuchs took the lead as keyboardist and composed nearly all of the tracks. With the launch of the Fuchs project about ten years ago, the roles reversed, bringing Hans and his guitars to the forefront with a more prominent role in the songwriting. But make no mistake: the role of his partner, Ines, remains essential. This is especially true on the album *Too Much Too Many*, their fourth to be released under the name Fuchs, where the balance between their respective contributions seems to be at its best.From the flamboyant "opening track" of the band's first album, *Ines* (Hunting The Fox ? 1994), to the irresistible "How I Wish That You Would"?sweetly sung by In�s Fuchs herself?which closed *Slipping Into The Unknown* eight years later, the flamboyant style of Genesis took center stage, as well as the neo-prog of IQ or Asgard (each album, incidentally, featuring members of that brilliant Italian band), but with a softer, more feminine touch provided by In�s's particularly sensual keyboards, her enchanting harmonies, and her warm, instantly recognizable solos?deeply inspired by those of Tony Banks.On Fuchs' albums, these musical influences seem to have been more fully assimilated and reimagined, to the point where *Too Much Too Many* opens with "Don't Get Me Wrong"?a stunning example of neo-prog, solid and well-grounded, enhanced by beautiful vocal harmonies. The influence of Genesis at its best is still evident throughout the album, particularly on "Once Again" and its sublime synth solo, but overall, *Too Much Too Many* presents a more personal and varied form of symphonic prog?without any jarring surprises, yet one that consistently provides a sense of well-being for the listener. The album alternates between deep, melancholic tracks, with pastel tones drifting on a gentle evening breeze ("Of Hopes And Dreams And Bitter Tears"), others with brighter colors that seem to gush from a warm spring ("Challenge of Lifelong Learning"), arrangements that are constantly in motion ("The Middle Years"), harmonies as beautiful as stars that seem to light up one by one in the sky ("My Life"), and supremely successful melodies, such as on the superbly epic progressive track "Here in My Void " (12:18)?the album's undisputed highlight, which evokes both the Camel of the nineties and the most melancholic RPWL, and in which every note, however varied in form and appeal, seems to surge powerfully in the same direction, straight toward the goal of auditory pleasure. In an era when sanitized pop sells by the millions and is viewed by the billions on YouTube, it's reassuring to know that music as profound, rich, and sincere as Fuchs's continues to exist?more alive than ever with *Too Much Too Many*, a work boldly crafted with passion and talent to better embrace under-explored facets of the soul.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Styx is an American prog-AOR band, a mix of Kansas (but less prog), Queen (but less grandiloquent), Boston (but less pompous), Slade (but less glam-rock), and Journey (but less Hard FM). Artistically speaking, then, is Styx simply a "less-than" band whose place in the Big Bang would be debatable?if not dispensable? That would be to dismiss a bit too hastily the two albums mentioned above and perhaps a handful of others that one might view with kindness (or even leniency) as partial successes in progressive rock. Moreover, every year since their self-titled debut album in 1972, Styx has managed to deliver a quarter-hour of more or less well-crafted symphonic prog?one or two tracks that still catch our attention today, even if they're buried in conventional rock of little interest. That famous quarter-hour became increasingly interesting over the years and across successive albums, culminating in *The Grand Illusion*, the most overtly progressive album in their discography. Probably capitalizing on a certain resurgence of public interest in this style of music these days (their album *The Mission* reached No. 45 on the U.S. sales charts in 2017), Styx has decided to stay on a path close to progressive rock and released *Crash of the Crown* in the summer of 2021. Shaw is omnipresent in the songwriting, sometimes aided by Gowen and especially by producer Will Evankovich, whose significant contributions at every level?composition, arrangements, and additional guitars and keyboards?were instrumental in achieving a dynamism that seems to give this band, now in its fifties, the wings of its youth. The first three tracks speak volumes, blending the melodic quality of Utopia with the energetic verve of Queen at their best, with Freddy Mercury's vocal style also taking center stage on the title track. "Hold Back the Darkness" is even more progressive, with its Pink Floyd-esque effects, a Roger Waters-style verse, and a guitar solo that seems to be a nod to *The Wall*. The homage to The Who is even more explicit with the VC3 synth intro to "To Those" or the middle section of "Common Ground," which seems straight out of *Quadrophenia*, vocal timbre and all. Despite this strong reference, these two tracks remain quintessentially Styx, with characteristic vocal parts that wouldn't have been out of place on *Pieces of Eight* or *The Grand Illusion*. The rest of the album is fairly conventional, although the Hammond organ solo on "Sound the Alarm" and the surprising dark-wave atmosphere of "Long Live the King" (it sounds as if Lisa Gerard is playing the yangqin) are capable of holding our attention for quite some time. *Crash of the Crown* is far from matching the successes of *The Grand Illusion* or *Pieces of Eight*, but this seventeenth studio album holds its own in Styx's extensive discography and confirms, following *The Mission* and before *Circling From Above* in 2025, that the Americans have finally moved beyond the unimaginative stadium rock that was their stock in trade in the '90s. That said, all things considered, by once again failing to fully realize the intentions we tend to attribute to the band (making mainstream yet powerful progressive rock), *Crash Of The Crown* doesn't change the overall picture. Styx remains a likable, high-energy melodic rock band that, despite its enjoyment of using varied arrangements and styles, is not yet ready to fully embrace its initial inclinations toward more elaborate music. This isn't necessarily a drawback (not playing prog isn't a flaw), but it may dissuade many of us from giving this album more than a casual, occasional listen.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most unique and stranger acts to emerge from the 70s prog scene was bizarre in many waysactually. AKASHA emerged from Norway, a nation currently prolific to progressive music in the 21stcentury wasn't a major player in the golden years of prog rock. And this band didn't come from Oslo,This short-lived act came from one of the most northern regions of all of Europe and formed in thesmall Arctic fishing village of Kj�llefjord. But what makes this band strange is that it reallydidn't sound like any other act of the day despite smatterings of influences piled into the schizoidrandom musical styles that seemed to find bits and pieces derived from Genesis, Pink Floyd, TheMoody Blues and King Crimson amongst others. The band was a quintet featuring Sverre Svendsen onlead vocals and mellotrons, Jens Ivar Andreassen on guitars, Mellotron, synthesizers, piano, organ,Arild Andreassen on bass, Kjell Evensen on drums and also included are the lyrics and poetry of Tor-Jony Hansen. AKASHA released only one mere album in 1977 and given its extreme remote location with littleopportunity for promotion or touring for that matter, the album has become one of those extremerarities. The strange artifact is also unique in that it displays the track listings on the frontcover but what really sets this one apart is the mishmash of music sounds that include hypnoticspace rock, freaky sound generated through synthesizers and mellotrons and a schizophrenic hairpinpropensity to simply morph into other music styles midstream reminding me a bit of the GermanKrautrock act Silberbart albeit with less guitar bombast. Likewise the band recorded in a bomb-proofcellar which was used as a shelter in the basement of a hotel in the small town of Finnsnes, Norwaywhich gives the production an interesting uniqueness much in the way of the band German Oak whichrecorded in a similar bomb shelter.The lengthy "Isle Of Kawi" begins the epic journey sounding something like the French Archaĩa withrapid fire synthesized arpeggios and what sounds like some sort of folk music but then sort ofshifts gears and sounds a bit more like something Pulsar would've conjured up on the first tworeleases. With this opening track it feels like you've stumbled into some lost classic musical treatas the sonic display is brooding and dark and on par with early Univers Zero for apocalyptic motifsof complete detachment from established paradigms. The track continues to morph into a labyrinthinedisplay of interesting twists and turns. The album quickly reveals its greatest flaw though on thesecond track "Bondage" which finds the lackluster vocal style of Sverre Svendsen who delivers arather mopey scatter-brained performance over some sort of drugged out lounge music before the trackbursts into rapid-fire key arpeggios that prognosticate the work of Philip Glass on "Glassworks" andhis classic "Koyaanisqatsi." And then off to some early "Trespass" styled Genesis sounding prog!The instrumental combo effect of "Recitativ" and "Electronic Nightmare" displays the band at itsmost unhinged with the first track in full rock mode for the first time only with strange guitarriffs and off-kilter contrapuntal elements. Unlike the prior tracks, this one has pounding drums anda guitar solo. The second on the other hand goes into outer space and features avant-gardeexperimentalism carried out through overlayering electronic effects sounding more Tangerine Dream orKlaus Schulze with a steady rhythmic pulse of Jean Michel Jarre. "Death Hymn" combines faster rockwith the electronics and then breaks into some sort of rockin' the classics keyboard freneticismmore in vein of The Nice. But wait! There's more - it then morphs into a slow oozing space rockmotif with detached spoken word lyrics which are in English. "Light And Darkness" is one of the mostschizoid tracks with several changes of tempos, styles and rich in off-kilter time signatures andjust plain bonkers ideas. More steeped in rock but drenched in mellotrons and atmospheric weirdnessas well."The Trip" offers the most normal track on board and actually sticks to a bluesy rock format formost of its run however the closing "Man And The Void" however returns to the restless nature of thealbum with a space rock intro that quickly shifts into strange guitar chord riffs and at timesreminds me of Gnidrolog but less structured and more freeform in many ways. This album offers thetrue spirit of DIY musical ambitions overcoming the extreme remote geography, lack of recordingfacilities and production extravaganzas. This band truly did things its own way on its own terms.Despite the imperfections of weak vocals, lackluster production and blatant disregard for any sortof unified sound, this album will appeal to those seeking out the most unapologetically originalalbums of the era and despite the flaws more than makes up for in its sheer creative audacity thatmakes AKASHA really a difficult band to classify with its symphonic prog, Krautrock and eclecticmusic spirit. For my tastes this one is quite appealing.

items.excerpt: Review by Hector Enrique — Following the iconic 2001 album "Blackwater Park", Opeth had planned to release a double album. However, encouraged by Jonas Renkse (Katatonia), the Swedish band led by Mikael ��kerfeldt decided to release two albums simultaneously, each with a distinct musical approach: "Damnation," more progressive and less aggressive -whose release was delayed once it was completed due to a commercial decision by the record label- and "Deliverance" (2002), which is likely one
items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Following the iconic 2001 album "Blackwater Park", Opeth had planned to release a double album. However, encouraged by Jonas Renkse (Katatonia), the Swedish band led by Mikael ��kerfeldt decided to release two albums simultaneously, each with a distinct musical approach: "Damnation," more progressive and less aggressive -whose release was delayed once it was completed due to a commercial decision by the record label- and "Deliverance" (2002), which is likely one of the band's heaviest, darkest, and most murky albums.Low tunings, thick distortion, persistent riffs, Martin Lopez's dizzying and at times excessive double-bass drumming, and ��kerfeldt's hellish guttural displays give the album its monolithic and brutal character, in tracks like the frenetic "Wreath" with its corrosive death metal sounds, the eponymous and superb "Deliverance," with its galloping and versatile riffs, hypnotic and hazy acoustic interludes, and a devastating instrumental finale led by guitarist Peter Lindgren, or the gothic darkness of "Master's Apprentices," featuring Steven Wilson's distinctive touch as he accompanies �kerfeldt with his melancholic voice and guitars.An atmosphere of extreme hostility from which "Deliverance" momentarily departs with "A Fair Judgment," which delves into the intricacies of progressive metal and evokes Floydian and Crimsonian influences in its structure, thickening in its final third with Lindgren's forceful, Black Sabbath-esque riffs -probably the best track on the album- and with the stripped-down "For Absent Friends," a brief and refreshing electro-acoustic tribute to the Genesis song of the same name, which offers a breather before the album plunges back into its darker textures.The experimental "By the Pain I See in Others" takes Opeth's progressive death metal into more twisted and dissonant territory, guided by �kerfeldt's cavernous and unsettling vocals to an intimidating new level and featuring a disconcerting circus-like middle section that evokes the grotesque theater of German composer Kurt Weill. After its musical development fades away, the track leaves a prolonged silence, interrupted by backward-played vocals from fragments of "Master's Apprentices," bringing the great album "Deliverance" to a close with a suspended, spectral echo.4 stars

Normally, I would like to assess each track; however, with an album like this, I find it difficult. There is a very strong sense of cohesion in "Dr. Aftershave." The songs blend very well, encouraging me to let the album play through in its entirety every time I go to listen. And while I also appreciate Missus Beastly' second and fourth albums, I think this one, "Dr. Aftershave," is the most consistent. As an album, it is the best. In my opinion, it does not have weaker tracks that I'd like to skip.

items.body: Hope I find you Awake tonight When I’m dreaming I can’t hold onto you Sleep offers a peculiar bargain to anyone missing someone they cannot reach. For a few hours, a face returns, a voice becomes clear, and the distance seems negotiable. Morning collects its debt. Louisville synth-pop trio MODISTE understands the terrible tenderness of that exchange, bringing a spellbinding ache to their cover of The Black Queen’s “Distanced.” Beautiful and uneasy in equal measure, their interpretation holds close to the original while allowing vocalist Sydney Sleadd to lead it somewhere distinctly her own. The cover’s release precedes MODISTE’s two upcoming appearances alongside The Black Queen and Trace Amount on the Fever Daydream tenth-anniversary tour. “Distanced” originally appeared on that album, and MODISTE have been performing it in their own sets since March. With the shared bills approaching, the trio moved quickly to have their recording mixed and mastered, turning a live favorite into a recorded salute before meeting its makers on the road. A tight, compressed snare rhythm and rippling bass synth establish the song’s measured movement. Sustained guitar accents stretch above them with a dreamy, Cure-like delicacy, leaving space for a voice that seems to glow in the dark. Sleadd’s singing carries warmth through an icy wash of reverb, her delivery intimate even as the room around it seems to expand. It is among MODISTE’s most Lynchian vocal turns yet: poised, emotionally exposed, and suggestive of a familiar room made strange by the person missing from it. As Sleadd begins to glide through the melody with greater force, the percussion gathers speed and the arrangement opens around her. Iridescent synth tones chime like fireflies in the dark; further layers rise beneath the chorus, lending weight to its plea for another encounter beyond waking life. Harmonies deepen that sense of yearning without crowding the lead. The guitar’s angular edges and the precision of the programmed drums keep the performance moving while the voice stretches toward something it cannot quite touch. The lyrics gradually reveal the severity of that separation. Songs, whispers, and the smallest intervals of consciousness become reminders of an absent person, until the reference to a grave makes the loss explicit. Sleep becomes both a means of reunion and another occasion for parting. Sleadd gives that contradiction room to hurt, building the chorus from a private wish into an appeal whose strength cannot guarantee an answer. The recording was mixed by Dave Chale at Louisville’s Deadbird Studios, becoming the first release mixed on the studio’s newly acquired Neve console. Chris Gehringer handled mastering at Sterling Sound. Listen to “Distanced” below: MODISTE brings together Sleadd, synthesist Dennis Stein, and guitarist Kyle Stallings. Sleadd’s background in Louisville’s folk songwriting community meets Stein’s more than 25 years of synth and production experience, including his solo work as Introvert, and Stallings’ grounding in punk, experimental rock, and electronic music. Working primarily with vintage analog synthesizers, drum machines, and digital instruments from the 1980s and 1990s, the trio draws connections between synth-pop, post-punk, new wave, and darker electronic music. Their debut album followed on August 7, 2026, and work on a second is already underway. Onstage, synchronized lighting, CRT televisions, glitch visuals, and avant-garde fashion extend the music’s peculiar atmosphere. Local photographers, seamstresses, designers, dancers, and videographers contribute to that wider creative world, giving the project a community beyond its three members. MODISTE Live dates with The Black Queen and Trace Amount: September 29 — Asheville, NC — Eulogy October 1 — Nashville, TN — Eastside Bowl More MODISTE live dates: October 2 — Adams, TN — Kinda Spoopy Fest at Red River Canoe Rental October 10 — Louisville, KY — Fall Schnitzelburg Walk at The Merryweather October 24 — Louisville, KY — “Night Service” at PORTAL (with MODELE, Black Signal, and Virgin Birth; Substance Subculture dance afterparty) Follow MODISTE: Website Instagram YouTube Spotify The post Louisville Synthpop Trio MODISTE Release Dreamy Cover of The Black Queen’s “Distanced” Ahead of Upcoming Tour Dates appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
